Jay Mody's [GPT in 60 Lines of NumPy](https://jaykmody.com/blog/gpt-from-scratch/)
is the clearest short explanation of GPT-2 inference I know of. It ends with a
section called *What Next?*, listing everything the 60 lines leave out: batching,
KV caching, sampling beyond greedy, training, evaluation, architecture
improvements.

That list is this series.

Two changes from the original. First, no NumPy. Mody gets `@`, broadcasting,
`np.split`, and a numerically sane `softmax` for free — which is exactly where the
confusion lives for most people reading these posts. We will write all of it by
hand, out of lists. Second, the series does not stop at a working forward pass.
The interesting engineering starts after that.

## Why removing NumPy is the point, not a stunt

When you write

``` python
x = x @ w + b
```

three things are hidden from you: how the multiply-accumulate is ordered, how `b`
gets stretched to match `x`, and what happens to precision along the way. When
you write the loop yourself, all three become decisions you have to make. That
matters later — by the time we add a KV cache and ragged batches, every bug will
be a shape bug or an indexing bug, and you cannot debug shapes you have never
had to construct.

So post 2 builds `matrix.py`: matmul, transpose, broadcast-add, softmax, mean and
variance. About a hundred lines, no imports. Everything after that is written
against it.

## But is it fast enough to actually use?

Worth answering before you invest a weekend in it. Here is the honest floor —
a tight triple loop, with the right operand pre-transposed so the inner loop
walks contiguous memory:

```{python}
#| label: bench
import time, random

def matmul(A, B_T, m, k, n):
    """A is (m, k). B_T is (n, k) — B pre-transposed so the inner loop is contiguous."""
    out = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(m)]
    for i in range(m):
        Ai, Oi = A[i], out[i]
        for j in range(n):
            Bj = B_T[j]
            s = 0.0
            for t in range(k):
                s += Ai[t] * Bj[t]
            Oi[j] = s
    return out

m, k, n = 16, 768, 768          # 16 tokens through one GPT-2-width projection
A   = [[random.random() for _ in range(k)] for _ in range(m)]
B_T = [[random.random() for _ in range(k)] for _ in range(n)]

t0 = time.perf_counter()
matmul(A, B_T, m, k, n)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0

macs = m * k * n
print(f"{macs/1e6:.1f}M multiply-accumulates in {elapsed:.2f}s")
print(f"{macs/elapsed/1e6:.1f}M MAC/s")
```

Call it ~25M MAC/s on one core. GPT-2 small is 124M parameters, so a single token
costs roughly 124M multiply-accumulates:

```{python}
#| label: extrapolate
rate = macs / elapsed
for name, params in [("GPT-2 small (124M)", 124e6), ("tiny model (~1M)", 0.9e6)]:
    print(f"{name:22s} {params/rate*1000:8.1f} ms/token")
```

So GPT-2 small runs at a few seconds per token in pure Python. Slow, but not
impossible — a forty-token completion is a coffee break, not an overnight job.
A ~1M-parameter model is effectively instant.

That sets the plan: **the tiny model is the workhorse, GPT-2 is the proof.** We
develop every mechanism on a 4-layer, 128-dimension model where the whole test
suite runs in under a second, and once per series we load the real OpenAI weights
and watch it produce English. Doing the engineering posts against GPT-2 would mean
a five-second wait on every iteration, which is how a series dies at post three.

## One rule for the series

Every post ends by proving the new version agrees with the old one. Not
"it looks right" — an actual assertion, with a tolerance:

``` python
def test_cache_matches_uncached(model, prompt, tol=1e-5):
    slow = [logits_for(model, prompt[:i+1])[-1] for i in range(len(prompt))]
    fast = logits_with_cache(model, prompt)
    for step, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(slow, fast)):
        worst = max(abs(x - y) for x, y in zip(a, b))
        assert worst < tol, f"step {step}: max abs diff {worst:.2e}"
```

Optimizations that silently change your outputs are the single most common
failure mode in inference code, and they are invisible unless you check. Writing
the check is a five-minute habit that will save you a weekend, and it is most of
what I do for a living.
